title: Unsupervised Diffusion Solver for Combinatorial Optimization via Combinatorial Adjoint Matching
claim: Our method reaches lower optimality gap than baselines at every inference budget, and keeps improving as sampling steps increase.
layout: single line plot, steps on x-axis, gap on y-axis, legend top-right
description: A single line chart titled 'Inference Scaling on MIS ER-[9000-11000]'. The x-axis shows inference steps (10, 20, 50, 100, 200) and the y-axis shows optimality gap in percent, from 0 to about 20. Four colored lines with distinct markers are shown: DiffUCO (blue circles), SDDS (green squares), RLNN (orange triangles), and CAM (purple diamonds). A legend sits in the top-right corner. RLNN starts very high, near 20% at 10 steps, and drops sharply. SDDS plateaus around 9%. DiffUCO and RLNN converge to roughly 2.5–3%. The purple CAM line stays lowest throughout, falling from about 3% to nearly 0%. Faint dashed gridlines are visible. The eye goes first to the steep orange drop, then to the purple line at the bottom.
caption: Comparison between CAM and baselines under different inference-time sampling budgets.
abstract: Diffusion-based neural solvers have shown strong promise for combinatorial optimization (CO), but existing methods typically rely on supervised training with large collections of near-optimal solutions. In this work, we extend adjoint-based trajectory optimization methods to discrete combinatorial domains. We formulate diffusion-based CO as a stochastic control problem over Continuous-Time Markov Chains and introduce discrete adjoint dynamics for propagating optimization signals through discrete generative trajectories. Building on this formulation, we propose Combinatorial Adjoint Matching (CAM), an unsupervised training framework for discrete diffusion solvers with structured and low-variance trajectory-level optimization signals. Empirically, CAM consistently outperforms existing unsupervised diffusion baselines and achieves performance competitive with strong supervised diffusion solvers and even traditional solvers across diverse combinatorial optimization problems. Our code is available at https://github.com/Shengyu-Feng/CAM.
